jobDescription:
Data Engineering Manager at The Economist Group
Writing SQL is one skill. Designing a data model that remains reliable as the business changes is another.
A strong model must handle changing customer attributes, late-arriving data, many-to-many relationships and aggregation without rewriting history or double-counting results.
Here are 10 data-modeling concepts every data engineer should be able to explain :
1. 𝗙𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘃𝘀 𝗗𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 -  the charged price is not always the list price
2. 𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 - define the atomic event before creating aggregates
3. 𝗦𝗖𝗗 𝗧𝘆𝗽𝗲 𝟮 - add a new version instead of overwriting history
4. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮 - start with the business process, not the entities
5. 𝗕𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀 - use allocation weights to prevent double-counting
6. 𝗟𝗮𝘁𝗲-𝗔𝗿𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗗𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 - create an inferred member instead of blocking facts
7. 𝗙𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗙𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗧𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀 - sometimes recording that an event occurred is enough
8. 𝗗𝗲𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗗𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 - identifiers such as `order_number` can remain on the fact
9. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿 𝘃𝘀 𝗦𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗸𝗲 - balance analytical simplicity with normalization
10. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗱 𝗗𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 - maintain one shared meaning of “customer” across business processes
The most important sentence to complete before drawing a model:
"𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 __________."
If that sentence is not clear, the model is not ready.
